idea: An app where campus event organizers post leftover food and students get notified to come grab it. Two of us, part-time (~12h/week each), 8 weeks, $300 budget. Must be free for students. Want a live map and push notifications.

nodes.label: Campus leftover-food sharing app
Organizers post leftover food (photo, location, pickup window)
nodes.rationale: Must-have: the supply side of the app

nodes.label: Student feed of available food
nodes.rationale: Students need one place to see what's available now

nodes.label: Push notifications for new food posts
nodes.rationale: Must-have: food goes fast, so students need to know immediately

nodes.label: SMS alerts for students without the app
nodes.rationale: Reaches students who won't install an app

objections.reason: SMS adds cost and consent/delivery complexity; validate student uptake with app push first.
Adds $250 in cost and is unnecessary for an initial app-based launch.
The $250 cost consumes most of the budget, and SMS consent and number handling add privacy work.

nodes.label: Live map of food locations
nodes.rationale: User asked for it; makes finding food in unfamiliar buildings easy

objections.reason: A custom live map is costly for an eight-week launch; retain useful location directions through the smaller text-and-link variant.
A live map adds substantial effort beyond the text location students need to find food.
A live map is not needed to test the core value and adds substantial build time.

nodes.label: Building and room shown as text, with a link to campus maps
nodes.rationale: Smaller variant of the live map: most of the value for 2h

nodes.label: Claim / reserve a portion
nodes.rationale: Prevents wasted trips when food is gone

objections.reason: Reservation state and handling add complexity; validate demand before building it.
Useful later for reducing wasted trips, but availability can be tested with a simple organizer update first.

nodes.label: In-app chat between organizers and students
nodes.rationale: Questions like 'is there any vegan food left?'

objections.reason: Chat introduces moderation and privacy work without being necessary for the core pickup flow.
Messaging is not needed to launch and expands moderation and implementation work.
Not essential to the pilot and increases moderation and privacy burden.

nodes.label: Campus email sign-in
nodes.rationale: Keeps the app to the campus community and deters abuse

nodes.label: Free for students
Allergen and dietary labels required on every post
nodes.rationale: Students with allergies must be able to decide safely

nodes.label: Food-safety liability (time since prepared, handling)
nodes.rationale: Posting checklist plus a pickup-window limit and disclaimer

nodes.label: Students may not trust food from strangers
nodes.rationale: Show the posting organization's name and verified campus email

evidence.title: Consumer food waste behaviour in universities: Sharing as a means of prevention
evidence.summary: A campus food-sharing intervention ran into barriers: trust, people's visceral relationship with food, and norms about acceptable food sources.

nodes.label: Hosting and domain
Which organizations will post first?
Food availability lifecycle: organizers can mark posts picked up or unavailable, and posts automatically expire at the pickup-window end
nodes.rationale: Keeps the feed, claims, and alerts from sending students to food that is no longer available.

nodes.label: Student report flow for inaccurate or concerning food posts, with a basic organizer/admin review queue
nodes.rationale: Provides a lightweight trust and safety response path for a campus pilot.

nodes.label: Managed backend foundation for posts, claims, campus-email auth, and web-push delivery
nodes.rationale: Use a managed database/auth service and a responsive web app to support the core flow without custom infrastructure.

nodes.label: End-to-end testing across posting, claiming, expiry, and notification flows
nodes.rationale: Validate the time-sensitive pickup journey and catch regressions before a campus pilot.

negotiation.message: I support a launch centered on verified posts, fast alerts, and accurate availability, with building-and-room directions instead of a custom map. negotiation.counteroffer: Ship the core campus food-sharing flow with text directions; defer costly and complex extras until the pilot validates demand.

negotiation.message: On r1-architect: Accept: it preserves the distinctive campus food-sharing and notification flow, replaces the expensive live map with useful text directions, and spends spare capacity on availability lifecycle, reporting, managed backend foundations, and end-to-end tests. Those additions make a pilot more reliable without exceeding the stated capacity or budget.

On r1-delivery: Reject: the plan preserves the core idea but uses only 52% of capacity and defers claims, leaving students exposed to wasted trips when food is gone. It also adds no explicit backend foundation, availability lifecycle, or end-to-end testing to make the time-sensitive flow reliable.

On r1-evidence: Accept: it keeps the core food-sharing and notification experience, improves the safety of allergen information by avoiding false assurances, and adds campus-policy validation before a pilot. Its main gaps are explicit availability lifecycle and testing work, but it remains a viable plan within the capacity and budget.

On r1-architect: Accept: lifecycle handling, reporting, backend foundations, and end-to-end tests reduce pilot risks. The 118-hour plan leaves limited capacity headroom, and the backend and web-push work deserve careful execution.

On r1-delivery: Accept: this is a lean, feasible core pilot with text directions and costly extras deferred. Without explicit post-expiry or reporting work, stale listings and trust issues remain risks, but the smaller scope is practical.

On r1-evidence: Accept: transparent ingredient and allergen disclosures avoid implying food is safe when information is unknown, and checking campus rules and organizer participation addresses key launch uncertainties. The core flow stays within the team's capacity.

On r1-architect: Accept: text directions preserve most map value, and expiry/status handling, reporting, and end-to-end tests strengthen the time-sensitive flow. The plan is within capacity, though it should also validate campus food rules and avoid suggesting required allergen labels establish safety.

On r1-delivery: Reject: this is a buildable narrow scope, but it leaves organizer participation unvalidated and lacks explicit expiry or status handling, so students may be notified about food that is no longer available. Those gaps weaken the core time-sensitive value of the pilot.

On r1-evidence: Accept: it preserves the must-haves and text directions while replacing potentially overconfident allergen labels with clear disclosures for unknown ingredients and allergens. Checking campus rules and starting with willing organizers is a concrete safeguard for an unvalidated pilot.
